candidateRows: A beginningless temporal series cannot exist because it would constitute an actually infinite collection, and actually infinite collections cannot exist in reality.
This is the formal core of Craig's actual-infinity argument for the finitude of the past and directly supports the debated Kalam premise.
After historical background and a distinction between Craig's two philosophical arguments, Craig states the syllogism based on the alleged impossibility of an actual infinite.
Hilbert's Hotel illustrates consequences so absurd that an actually infinite number of concrete things should be judged metaphysically impossible.
The hotel thought experiment supplies Craig's principal justification for the crucial premise that no actual infinite can be instantiated in reality.
Craig distinguishes potential from actual infinity, explains Cantorian collections, and uses fully occupied finite and infinite hotels to motivate his metaphysical conclusion.
Aristotle can consistently regard past and future time as infinite but merely potentially infinite because their infinitude is temporally distributed rather than simultaneously present.
This supplies a historically grounded alternative conception of infinity that challenges Craig's assumption that an infinite past must be an actual infinite.
Craig's distinction between actual and potential infinity and his classification of a beginningless past as actually infinite.
Malpass explains Aristotle's terminology, notes that a potential infinite never becomes actual, and accepts Craig's usage provisionally while marking the conceptual difference.

The strange consequences of infinite collections do not establish metaphysical impossibility unless an actual contradiction is derived, because apparent absurdity is not a reliable guide to possibility.
The objection attacks the inferential step from Hilbert-style counterintuitive consequences to the metaphysical impossibility of concrete actual infinities.
Craig's claim that Hilbert's Hotel demonstrates the metaphysical impossibility of any concrete actual infinite.
Malpass analyzes the shared Cantorian property behind hotel and library cases, contrasts absurdity with contradiction, and invokes empirically accepted quantum strangeness as a caution.

On a tensed theory of time, an infinite past cannot be merely potential because infinitely many events would already have elapsed, whereas an endless future always contains only finitely many realized events.
This proposed past-future asymmetry directly answers Malpass's Aristotelian alternative and preserves the premise that a beginningless past is actually infinite.
Malpass's claim that Aristotle can treat both an infinite past and an infinite future as potential rather than actual infinities.
Craig argues that real temporal succession proceeds toward later times, distinguishes mental backward counting from temporal progress, and contrasts elapsed past events with future addition.

Although actual infinities involve no formal contradiction, multiplying their concrete absurdities warrants judging them metaphysically impossible, and quantum mechanics provides no sound counterexample.
This defends the modal force of Craig's thought experiments against Malpass's central objection that counterintuitiveness alone does not demonstrate impossibility.
Malpass's contention that Hilbert-style absurdity is insufficient without contradiction and that quantum phenomena caution against modal judgments from strangeness.
Craig concedes the absence of logical contradiction, adds Benardete's infinitely paged book, rejects the quantum analogy as interpretation-dependent, and confines Cantorian infinity to concepts.

If an infinite past is impossible because it contains infinitely many events, temporal mirroring implies that an endless future is likewise impossible because it includes infinitely many future events.
The symmetry objection pressures Craig's actual-infinity argument by deriving a consequence apparently inconsistent with his acceptance of a possibly endless future.
Craig's argument that a beginningless past is impossible because it would comprise an actually infinite number of temporal events.
Malpass mirrors past and future using an immortal angel praising God daily, arguing that changing tense does not change the number of praises and requires a symmetry breaker.

The future-symmetry objection exposes no flaw in the argument for a finite past: it is either merely ad hominem against people committed to an endless future or question-begging about that future's possibility.
This is Craig's first direct defense against the symmetry objection and denies that its mirrored consequence undermines the reasoning for past finitude.
Malpass and Morriston's argument that Craig's reasoning against an infinite past applies with equal force against a possibly endless future.
Craig distinguishes direct from indirect criticism, limits the objection's force to people with relevant commitments, and says bare appeal to a possible endless future assumes what is disputed.

Anyone who infers from the impossibility of a beginningless past that an endless future is impossible must defend the radical modal thesis that no possible world has a temporal beginning without an end.
The burden-shifting argument challenges the symmetry objection by emphasizing the strength of the modal conclusion its proponent must accept and independently justify.
Malpass's temporal-mirroring inference from the alleged impossibility of a beginningless past to the impossibility of an endless future.
Craig formulates the objection's consequence in possible-world terms, repeats it for clarification, and characterizes denial of every beginning-without-end world as requiring substantial proof.
The parity objection rules out temporally asymmetric models unless an independent symmetry breaker is supplied, while leaving symmetric finite-finite and infinite-infinite models open.
This develops the central parity objection by specifying which temporal models survive and identifying the missing symmetry breaker required by Craig's position.
Craig's claim that parity between beginningless pasts and endless futures imposes an exceptionally radical modal burden on the objector.

After Craig presses the alleged burden of denying a beginning-without-end world, Malpass reframes the consequence as exclusion of asymmetric temporal structures rather than denial of every infinite temporal model.

A tensed theory supplies the relevant past-future asymmetry because future events do not yet exist and an endless future remains only potentially infinite, whereas a beginningless past cannot be potentially infinite in the same way.
This is Craig's principal answer to the parity objection and is necessary to reconcile his rejection of an infinite past with acceptance of an endless future.
Malpass's contention that, without a symmetry breaker, past and future must have matching finite or infinite modal structures.
Craig distinguishes an endless but always finite future from a beginningless past by appealing to objective temporal becoming and the absence of presently existing future events.

Past events can instantiate an actual infinite despite no longer existing because they have occurred in reality, whereas future events have never been instantiated and remain unreal on a tensed theory.
The distinction supplies the metaphysical basis for treating past and future differently and therefore underwrites Craig's response to the temporal parity objection.
The objection that presentism makes both past and future events nonexistent now, apparently restoring symmetry between the two directions.
Craig contrasts tensed and tenseless theories, conceding parity on a tenseless view but arguing that objective temporal becoming makes an endless future finite at every stage.

Presentism does not break temporal symmetry because past events no longer exist while future events will exist, and Craig's potential-infinity argument equivocates between simple future and future-perfect claims.
This directly attacks the proposed symmetry breaker and argues that the tense distinction supporting Craig's treatment of an endless future is linguistically and logically unstable.
Craig's argument that objective temporal becoming distinguishes instantiated past events from unreal future events and makes only the future potentially infinite.
Malpass argues that correctly matching past, future, and future-perfect tenses restores symmetry, illustrating the point with marbles added daily to a jar over an endless future.
Even if actual infinite collections are possible, the past cannot be actually infinite because an actual infinite cannot be formed through the successive addition by which temporal events accumulate.
This is the debate's second principal Kalam argument and directly supports the claim that the temporal past must be finite independently of objections to actual infinite collections.
Craig states a two-premise successive-addition argument, then supports it with the Jupiter-Saturn orbit comparison and a Grim Reaper construction said to yield contradiction.

The Jupiter-Saturn result reflects the ordinary cardinal behavior of infinite sets, while the real successive-addition issue is only that counting cannot reach a number lacking an immediate predecessor.
The response separates familiar infinite-cardinality behavior from the transition question and narrows what the impossibility of counting to infinity can legitimately establish about time.
Craig's successive-addition argument and its claim that the planetary-orbit illustration exposes absurdity in a beginningless accumulated past.
Malpass accepts that time cannot contain moments more than finitely distant from one another but argues that endless counting still covers every natural number in the relevant cardinal sense.

From the fact that an endless counter can count every particular natural number, it does not follow that he will count all natural numbers, because that inference shifts modal or quantifier scope and commits composition.
This challenges the key inference in Malpass's endless-counting reply and preserves the successive-addition argument by distinguishing distributive reachability from collective completion.
Malpass's claim that an endless counter's ability to count each natural number supports saying that the counter counts the entire infinite collection.
Craig uses counting, traversal, and composition examples to argue that each member's finite accessibility cannot establish that the whole infinite series is successively traversable.

Showing that every-to-all inferences sometimes fail does not show failure in the endless-counting case, where counting each natural number appears to make counting all of them a truth-preserving conclusion.
The reply contests whether Craig has diagnosed any fallacy in the specific inference under dispute and thus keeps the cardinal endless-counting objection alive.
Craig's assertion that moving from the ability to count every particular number to counting all numbers is a scope or composition fallacy.
Malpass contrasts invalid naming and motherhood examples with potentially valid whole-loaf reasoning, then argues that uninterrupted endless counting resembles the latter rather than the former.
Successive counting can never convert a potential infinite into an actual infinite, as Tristram Shandy can leave no particular page unwritten without ever completing the entire autobiography.
This supplies a concrete countermodel to Malpass's claimed every-to-all inference and restates the mechanism at the heart of the successive-addition argument.
Malpass's insistence that, in uninterrupted endless counting, counting every natural number makes it legitimate to say that all natural numbers are counted.

Craig argues that infinite sets must be given tenselessly rather than generated temporally, illustrating the distinction through an autobiography with every page eventually written but never completed.

Craig's appeal to potential infinity relies on future-perfect claims about how many numbers will have been counted, which does not settle the distinct simple-future claim that every number will be counted.
The tense distinction targets the logical form of Craig's Tristram Shandy response and offers a direct explanation of why finite completion at every stage need not defeat endless coverage.
Craig's claim that successive addition only yields a potential infinite and that Tristram Shandy can address every page without completing all pages.

Malpass explains future-perfect tense through a drinking example, concedes that no stage contains a completed infinity, and argues that Craig illegitimately transfers that result to simple-future claims.
The reverse-counting objection appears to combine a sufficient-reason challenge with a distinct claim that an eternal counter should already have finished at every earlier time.
This separates two possible arguments within Craig's successive-addition case and requests clarification of the inference that allegedly makes a beginningless countdown impossible.
Craig's contention that completing a countdown from infinity is impossible because the counter should already have finished.
After moving from an endless future count to the more relevant beginningless-past analogy, Malpass distinguishes an explanatory objection from an already-finished objection.

A beginningless countdown is incoherent because at every past point the counter has already had infinitely much time and therefore should already be finished, contradicting the hypothesis that he was still counting.
The move directly defends the successive-addition argument by explaining both the already-finished contradiction and the later role of a modest principle of sufficient reason.
Malpass's proposal that Craig may be conflating two distinct objections to a completed beginningless countdown.

Craig presents the argument as a sequence: an infinite amount of prior counting should suffice for completion, while denying an explanation for the chosen endpoint triggers a modest sufficient-reason response.
Having counted for infinitely many past moments is necessary for finishing an infinite countdown now, but it is not sufficient, since the counter could currently have any finite remainder.
This attacks the key modal inference in Craig's successive-addition defense: infinite elapsed counting time does not entail completion at the present or any earlier point.
Craig's claim that infinitely much elapsed counting time means the beginningless counter should already have completed the countdown.
Malpass corrects what he regards as an ordering error between conditions for present completion and argues that Craig's use of 'should' is modally too strong.
An infinite amount of time paired one-to-one with the numbers appears sufficient for completing the countdown, unless one denies that its particular finishing time requires an explanation.
The response defends the disputed sufficiency inference and identifies the principle of sufficient reason as the remaining route for excluding an arbitrary completion point.
Malpass's distinction between infinite past counting as a necessary condition and as a sufficient condition for finishing now.
Craig maintains that infinite time plus correspondence between moments and counted numbers leaves no evident missing condition, then shifts the dispute to explanation of the endpoint.
A modest demand for partial explanation can be satisfied by local facts about the counter's recent state and counting rate, even if those facts do not remove every further explanatory mystery.
This challenges Craig's fallback sufficient-reason argument by offering the kind of partial explanation that the modest principle appears to require without explaining the entire infinite history.
Craig's claim that a plausible modest principle of sufficient reason requires an explanation of why the countdown ends now rather than earlier.
Malpass contrasts overly strong explanation with partial explanation, illustrates how explanatory mystery can be displaced, and applies that model to the final minutes of the countdown.
The relevant modest principle of sufficient reason is nevertheless violated by a beginningless counter finishing at one time rather than another because no adequate explanation selects that endpoint.
This preserves the explanatory branch of Craig's successive-addition defense against Malpass's proposed local explanation and states the exact alleged defect of the scenario.
Malpass's proposal that the counter's finite remaining numbers and fixed counting rate provide an adequate partial explanation.
Craig declines to reconstruct the full published principle from memory but insists that it is modest, defensible, and not satisfied by an arbitrary finishing point.

For this discussion, an actually infinite collection is one whose proper part can be placed in one-to-one correspondence with the whole, although other philosophical communities add further conditions.
The shared definition fixes the central concept used throughout the actual-infinity dispute and clarifies that the parties are not primarily divided over terminology.
In audience questions, Malpass notes broader disputes between actualists and potentialists but adopts the Cantorian proper-part criterion as the operative definition here.
Grim Reaper arguments may face an accumulation-related fallacy and can potentially be temporally mirrored so that reasoning used for a beginning of time also implies an end of the future.
The proposed temporal mirror challenges the asymmetry required by paradox-based arguments for a finite past, though Malpass explicitly treats the development as tentative.
The audience-presented Grim Reaper and Hilbert's-hotel argument intended to rule out a beginningless sequence of events.
Malpass cannot reconstruct the cited premise numbering, refers to a published response, and sketches a tentative future-end parallel to beginning-of-time paradox arguments.

Causal finitism avoids the alleged past-future parallel because no event can result from infinitely many causes, excluding a beginningless causal past without excluding an endless forward causal series.
The argument supplies a structurally asymmetric alternative defense of a finite past that directly answers Malpass's strategy of temporally mirroring finitude arguments.
Malpass's contention that Grim Reaper-style reasoning for a temporal beginning may be mirrored to imply a future endpoint.
Craig recommends causal finitism as an alternative to full finitism: it limits the number of causes of an event while permitting causes to continue indefinitely forward.
Malpass's position is skeptical rather than beginningless-past advocacy: undermining arguments for a cosmic beginning does not require establishing that the universe had no beginning.
This defines the con side's burden on the debate's central question: the target is the adequacy of Kalam support, not proof that the universe is beginningless.
Asked whether his objections are the strongest case against a beginning, Malpass says he offers no positive beginningless-past argument and instead seeks to disarm Craig's support.
A backward-infinite sequence does not entail a possible Hilbert's Hotel when only finitely many rooms can be created at any one time.
This directly challenges a premise in a reformulated actual-infinity argument intended to establish that a backward-infinite past is impossible.
Alexander Pruss's claim that a backward-infinite event sequence would make Hilbert's Hotel possible.
After the moderator presents Pruss's Hilbert's Hotel and Grim Reaper formulation, Malpass invokes a finite-at-each-time creation restriction to deny its first premise.
Several reformulations of the infinity argument avoid the past-future symmetry objection raised against Craig's preferred formulation.
The move argues that Malpass's symmetry criticism does not defeat the broader family of philosophical arguments for a finite past.
Malpass's symmetry-based critique and his response to Pruss's alternative Hilbert's Hotel formulation.
Craig connects the exchange to his earlier replies and points to formulations by Hedrick, Loke, and Pruss that allegedly escape the symmetry objection.
Counting indefinitely remains merely potentially infinite because every finite number can be reached without ever completing all natural numbers.
The distinction between endless finite progression and completed infinity is foundational to the successive-addition case for a beginning of the past.
The audience suggestion that counting past every natural number amounts to counting infinitely many items.
In response to an indefinite-counting question, Craig says that each finite natural number may be counted while the totality is never completed or reached.
The relevant claim is that every individual number will be counted, not that counting eventually finishes at a completed endpoint called infinity.
This preserves the con side's successive-addition objection by separating distributive coverage of every member from completion of an infinite task.
Craig's claim that indefinite counting never reaches or completes infinity and therefore remains potential.
Malpass argues that Craig again substitutes the absence of a final completed stage for the distinct question whether each natural number gets counted.
From every member being finitely distant or eventually counted, one cannot infer that all members collectively form a completed finite totality.
This alleges the core quantifier error on which Craig says Malpass's challenges to both counting and an infinite past repeatedly depend.
Malpass's inference from each natural number eventually being counted to the significance of counting infinitely many.
Craig distinguishes facts about each finite member from facts about the whole infinite series and labels Malpass's recurring inference illicit.
The alleged every-to-all fallacy has not been demonstrated, and a worked countermodel is needed before Malpass should accept Craig's diagnosis.
The move rejects Craig's principal diagnosis of the con argument and identifies the missing demonstration needed to resolve their central impasse.
Craig's accusation that Malpass repeatedly commits an illicit inference from every member to all members.
Malpass acknowledges an impasse but maintains that Craig has not shown the alleged fallacy and asks for a concrete countermodel of the inference.
The Grim Reaper argument is the most difficult relevant challenge for Malpass to resolve and remains an unsettled puzzle in his analysis.
The concession identifies a reformulated infinity-based argument as a serious unresolved pressure point for the con position despite its broader skepticism.
Asked which theistic arguments he finds most compelling, Malpass singles out the Grim Reaper argument as unusually resistant to settled resolution.
A tenseless theory is compatible with a cosmic beginning, and astrophysical evidence may support an earlier spacetime boundary despite endless future expansion.
This protects the beginning claim from dependence on a tensed theory while distinguishing a finite past boundary from a potentially infinite future.
Craig answers a compatibility question by separating logical temporal theory from empirical cosmology and describing a bounded past with potentially endless expansion.
The Kalam case is strongly supported because causation, philosophical finite-past arguments, and astrophysical evidence jointly imply a personal transcendent creator.
This is Craig's closing synthesis of the premises, the philosophical and scientific support for a cosmic beginning, and the inferred divine cause.
Craig closes by combining the causal premise, the debated philosophical arguments, expansion and thermodynamic evidence, and properties attributed to the universe's cause.
The Kalam conclusion requires controversial commitments about tense and inference, while the central disagreement remains unresolved rather than adequately rebutted.
Malpass's closing assessment challenges the adequacy of the philosophical support by stressing controversial prerequisites and the failure to resolve the central inference dispute.
Craig's defense of the tense-based Kalam argument and his claim that Malpass's reasoning commits an every-to-all error.
Malpass closes by emphasizing controversy over temporal theory, possible mutual misunderstanding, and the absence of a resolution adequate to defeat his objection.
